extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media researchers, policymakers, and the general public interested in press regulation in India
extracted.subtask_description: Wikipedia article describing the statutory Press Council of India: its objectives, composition, Code of Ethics (Norms of Journalistic Conduct), complaints mechanism, and findings on paid news and related transparency issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective: preserving freedom of the press and improving standards
rubrics_metrics.description: "preserving the freedom of the press by maintaining and improving the standards of newspapers and the news agencies" (objective of the Press Council of India as re-established by the Press Council Act, 1978).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the Council's mandate as protecting press freedom while also promoting journalistic standards; grounds the PCI as a statutory and quasi-judicial body (re-established 1979; initially set up 1966).

rubrics_metrics.name: Council composition and appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: The council has a chairman – traditionally, a retired Supreme Court judge, and 28 additional members of which 20 are members of media, nominated by the newspapers, television channels and other media outlets operating in India. In the 28 member council, 5 are members of the lower house (Lok Sabha) and upper house (Rajya Sabha) of the Indian parliament and three represent culture literary and legal field as nominees of Sahitya Academy, University Grant Commission and Bar Council of India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies statutory/expected makeup and nominee sources for the Press Council, indicating representational balance between media, parliament, and cultural/legal institutions; useful as a procedural standard for legitimacy and stakeholder representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms of Journalistic Conduct (Code of Ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Press Council of India has issued the 'Norms of Journalistic Conduct', which is one of two journalism-related codes in use in India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as the PCI's formal code of ethics for journalists and publications; functions as guiding standards for content, conduct, and professional behaviour (the page does not reproduce the full norms but identifies them as the Council's primary ethical code).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaints handling powers and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Press Council of India accepts complaints against and by the press in matters relating to a journalist's or media organisation's ethical failures. The council can investigate and issue a report. It also can 'warn, admonish, censure or disapprove' those it finds at fault, but it has no powers to enforce nor impose any penalty on individual journalists and publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the scope of PCI's remedial and adjudicatory functions (investigation, reporting, non-binding sanctions like censure). Example: on 21 July 2006 the Council censured three newspapers for violation of norms. Emphasizes limitation: PCI cannot impose legal penalties or enforce sanctions beyond moral/administrative censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and forms of 'paid news'
rubrics_metrics.description: PCI's 2010 report described 'paid news' as a pervasive, structured and highly organised practice where news space and favourable coverage is exchanged for money. It ranges from accepting gifts, foreign and domestic junkets, various monetary and non-monetary benefits, besides direct payment of money, to 'private treaties' where a media company receives shares from a non-media company in lieu of advertisement space and favourable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides concrete categories/examples of unethical practices that constitute paid news, useful for identifying violations: gifts, trips, monetary/non-monetary benefits, direct payments, and corporate-media private treaties transferring shares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid news findings and recommended/proscribed practices
rubrics_metrics.description: PCI's 2010 investigation (limited to the 2009 elections) found substantial evidence of corrupt practices and collusion between the Indian media, various politicians and political parties. It ruled that newspapers should not carry articles that report 'enmity or hatred between people on the ground of religion, race, caste, community or language', should refrain from critical statements on 'personal character and conduct of a political candidate', and should refuse financial or indirect forms of compensation for political coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are voluntary guidelines/proscriptions aimed at protecting electoral fairness and journalistic integrity. They function as evaluative criteria for whether coverage is ethical (e.g., avoid hate-inciting content, avoid undisclosed paid political coverage, avoid personal-character attacks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and public availability of investigation reports
rubrics_metrics.description: An RTI application seeking a copy of the PCI's paid-news report was rejected by the PCI; the Central Information Commission (CIC), however, ordered the PCI to provide the report to the applicant and also make it publicly available on its website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates an expectation (enforced via CIC) that PCI investigation reports should be transparent and publicly accessible; relevant as a procedural standard for accountability and public scrutiny of the Council's findings.
